transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-20
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (Lumen ML Platform Lead), Priya Singh (Lumen Director of ML), Ethan Cole (Lumen Infra)

Summary: (auto) quick intro, then deep dive on quantization techniques, followed by pilot plan and next steps. Some transcription glitches present.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, and Samira is our SE. How's everyboday doing?
[00:08] Mark Rivera: Doing good, thanks. We wanna get into quantization choices—we're seeing big cost spikes with our 13B models in production.
[00:16] Samira Patel: Great, we'll run through INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ, and tradeoffs. Also how that interacts with batching and KV cache, and options for Dedicated vs on-prem.
[00:25] Priya Singh: Side note, our primary concern is accuracy regressions on safety-critical prompts, so we need tight evals.
[00:33] Samira: Absolutely, we'll talk measurables and how to pin regressions.

[00:40] Alex Chen: Quick qual: what's your infra setup today? GPUs, inference pattern?
[00:45] Ethan Cole: We're running a mix, mostly A10G for dev and V100 in prod, using Triton internally for some endpoints. Latency target is 200ms p95 for short chat turns, throughput for batch jobs is higher.
[00:58] Samira: Ok A10/V100 is helpful context. Some of the quantization kernels behave differently across Ampere vs Volta.

[01:10] Mark: Also, we do hybrid workloads: streaming chat + long-context summarization. So KV cache usage is heavy for the chat flows.
[01:18] Samira: Important—KV cache and quantization sometimes cause higher memory pressure or reduced KV sharing efficiency. We'll cover mitigations.

[02:05] Samira: Starting with basics: INT8 gives the biggest model size and throughput improvements when supported. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quant methods that often produce near-FP16 quality but with different complexity and hardware compatibility.
[02:20] Mark: Can you explain AWQ vs GPTQ quickly? We've seen both in bench notes but not clear differences.
[02:28] Samira: Sure. GPTQ focuses on layer-wise quantization with per-channel scales and typically requires more compute to produce quant files but is pretty mature for autoregressive models. AWQ is newer, uses adaptive weight quant, often preserves accuracy better on some models and can be more amenable to INT8-like runtimes. But A W Q results vary by model and prompt distribution.
[02:45] Priya: We care about edge cases—rare prompts that trigger hallucinations. How do you measure regressions?
[02:51] Samira: We recommend a test harness: holdout prompt set (Priya's prompts), fuzzy matching tolerances, and per-prompt scoring (e.g., BLEU-ish or embedding-similarity). Also track safety-related signal bits separately.

[03:40] Ethan: Any hardware caveats? We saw FP8 hype but not sure support matrix.
[03:46] Samira: FP8 yields promising accuracy/size tradeoffs, but hardware/software support is patchy. Ampere doesn't have native FP8 kernels; Hopper/TensorCores on H100 have better FP8 perf. For most cloud fleets, INT8 quant with optimized kernels gives more consistent throughput wins.

[04:20] Alex: Real world example—on model X (13B variant) our internal bench saw GPTQ-INT8 at ~3.2x throughput and 2.8x cost reductions, with 1.5-2% Rouge-L drop on summarization. Is that acceptable?
[04:36] Priya: 2% drop could be big for us on certain flows. We need a breakdown by prompt type.
[04:43] Samira: That's why we'll run per-prompt buckets. Also AWQ sometimes reduces that delta to <1% but may increase runtime quant artifact size or slightly different latency.

[05:10] Mark: KV cache—does quantization change cache hit/miss behavior?
[05:16] Samira: Not directly, but quantized runtimes sometimes shard KV differently to optimize memory, which can alter eviction patterns. Also smaller model weights can enable larger batch KV regions in memory, improving hit rates if configured properly.
[05:34] Ethan: So we might need to tune cache sizing and eviction if we move to INT8.
[05:37] Samira: Exactly. Redwood's runtime exposes KV cache sizing and auto-eviction heuristics you can tune per-route. We'll recommend starting with conservative settings and monitor p95 latency.

[06:00] Alex: Batching tradeoffs — customers often ask for big batch sizes to maximize throughput, but that hurts latency for streaming. How are you handling that?
[06:10] Mark: We usually set separate endpoints: low-latency chat routes with small batch and lower CPU overhead, and batch jobs for offline processing.
[06:17] Samira: That's a good pattern. Also Redwood supports adaptive batching thresholds and soft timeouts, so short chat can remain low-latency while background pools handle large batch windows. Quantization sometimes changes the optimal batch size — INT8 kernels scale better with larger batches.

[07:05] Priya: Any observed accuracy regressions that are prompt-length dependent?
[07:11] Samira: Yes, longer contexts can amplify quantization noise due to accumulation in attention scores and layernorm. So for long-context summarization you might prefer FP16 or mixed precision. For short-turn chat, INT8/GPTQ often looks fine.

[08:00] Mark: On-prem / VPC concerns — we need to keep keys on-prem and have audit logs. How does Redwood handle KMS/HSM?
[08:10] Alex: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS, support HSM-backed keys, and provide audit log exports. We'll share the security packet—Samira will include specific compliance notes.
[08:22] Ethan: Performance-wise, does running Private affect kernel choices?
[08:26] Samira: The runtime is the same, but on-prem hardware differences (e.g., older GPUs) can constrain use of FP8. We can ship optimized kernels for your hardware; we'll need sample environment details.

[09:00] Samira: Let's go through a proposed pilot: take your 13B model, produce GPTQ and AWQ quantized variants, run Redwood Dedicated pilot with identical workload replay using your prompt sets, and collect token-level latency, output diffs, and accuracy scores.
[09:15] Mark: Sounds good. How long to produce quantized variants?
[09:20] Samira: GPTQ run for a 13B can take a few hours on a GPU, AWQ similar but depends on tooling. We'll do this in partnership — you can share the model artifact or we can do it in your VPC.
[09:33] Alex: We'll need permissions and an S3 link or on-prem transfer. We'll create a secure presigned flow.

[10:10] Priya: Are there known model families with bad GPTQ outcomes?
[10:14] Samira: Some MoE or heavily tuned instruction-tuned variants have larger deltas. Also models with per-head scaling quirks sometimes show instability at 8-bit. We'll stress test those.

[11:00] Mark: Bench numbers — can you share typical p95 latency changes when moving to INT8 on A10 vs V100?
[11:07] Samira: Roughly, on A10 you might see 20-35% p95 reduction, on V100 it's less pronounced. H100 with FP8 can beat those but depends on kernel maturity. We'll send micro-benchmarks.

[12:05] Alex: Question about rolling back: if we detect regressions in production, how do fallbacks work?
[12:10] Samira: Redwood's routing supports automatic fallback to FP16 variant per-request or per-route; you can configure thresholds (accuracy delta or confidence) to switch. We also support canary rollouts at traffic percentages.

[13:00] Priya: For evaluation, we'd like per-prompt deltas and diffs stored. Can Redwood annotate outputs and keep artifacts for later analysis?
[13:07] Samira: Yes, we can persist outputs and metadata per request for a retention period (configurable), and attach eval metrics. We'll include an eval harness template.

[14:00] Mark: Anything specific about tokenizer interactions with quant? We've seen token-level shifts.
[14:07] Samira: Tokenizer mismatch isn't caused by quant per se, but subtle numerical differences can change generation branching which appears as token shifts. That's expected; evaluation via embeddings similarity is often more robust than exact token match.

[15:00] Ethan: On the ops side, memory footprint reductions from INT8 — what's realistic for 13B?
[15:05] Samira: Model weight size can drop ~2x from FP16 to INT8; memory for KV cache might dominate for long contexts, but total GPU memory usage often drops, enabling larger batch/longer context if you tune.

[16:10] Alex: Customer question: can AWQ and GPTQ be combined or ensembled?
[16:15] Samira: Some customers run ensemble routing—try AWQ in low-latency paths and GPTQ for batch. Ensemble at token-level is tricky. Redwood supports multi-variant routing and A/B tests.

[17:00] Mark: About accuracy metrics: is there an established threshold you recommend to accept quantized variant?
[17:07] Samira: It depends on the workload. For general chat, customers accept <1% embedding similarity loss or <2% task metric delta. Safety-critical flows usually require <0.5% or manual review. We'll help set thresholds per-prompt bucket.

[18:20] Priya: For the pilot, we want transparent token-level cost. Can you show us cost delta and a per-route breakdown?
[18:28] Alex: Yes Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency per route; we'll also produce a comparison spreadsheet for the pilot.

[19:15] Mark: Any gotchas with Triton on-prem? We currently wrap Triton endpoints.
[19:21] Samira: Triton has its own optimizations; integrating quantized kernels requires plugin work. If you're using Redwood Private, we handle runtime directly. If you keep Triton, we'll coordinate on compatible artifacts.

[20:05] Ethan: Logs and audit — we'll need SOC2 scopes. Can you share compliance docs?
[20:10] Alex: We'll send the security packet and SOC2 summary after the call.

[21:00] Samira: Quick deep dive—example of an attention score drift: in INT8, small rounding in matmul leads to slightly different softmax distributions. Over repeated layers that can nudge outputs. For long context this compounds. So we instrument layer outputs during the pilot to detect drift windows.

[22:00] Mark: How intrusive is that instrumentation?
[22:04] Samira: It's lightweight for a pilot; we log selected layer activations for a sample set. Not something you'd keep in prod continuously.

[23:00] Priya: How will we compare AWQ vs GPTQ results?
[23:04] Samira: We'll run identical prompts, capture outputs, compute embedding-similarity, task metrics, evaluate safety signals, and present per-prompt deltas. Also compute cost/throughput tradeoff table.

[25:00] Alex: Operational timeline — propose: this week share artifact links and prompt sets, next week Redwood creates quant variants and runs 48-hour replay on Dedicated, following week we review results and plan rollouts.
[25:12] Priya: That timeline works for us.

[26:00] Mark: A couple of smaller concerns — reproducibility when quantizing across different seed runs. Do you see variance?
[26:07] Samira: There is some non-determinism in quantization tooling; we fix seeds and document env to get reproducible runs. We'll keep hash of quant artifacts.

[28:00] Ethan: Network egress for on-prem pilot — we need to limit external calls. Can Redwood operate fully in VPC?
[28:06] Alex: Yes Redwood Private operates with a customer-managed control plane and no egress if required. We'll include network diagrams.

[30:00] Samira: Quick note on GK cache: if you mean KV cache, we sometimes see small accuracy benefits by pre-warming cache with prefix embeddings; that behavior is stable across quant modes but requires route-level prewarm.

[31:00] Mark: Any recommended hyperparams to re-train or finetune to recover accuracy?
[31:06] Samira: Sometimes small lo-fi calibration (bias correction) or layer-wise QAT can help, but that increases engineering cost. Post-training methods like GPTQ/AWQ are lower effort. We'll document options.

[34:00] Priya: Ok, let's recap concrete next steps.
[34:05] Alex: 1) Samira send AWQ/GPTQ microbenchmarks and instrumentation plan. 2) Alex send Dedicated pilot pricing and security packet. 3) Priya provide 3 prompt sets and success metrics. 4) Samira run quantization and Redwood runs replay.
[34:20] Priya: I'll get the prompts by Monday/Wednesday.

[35:00] Mark: Any paperwork for Dedicated pilot?
[35:05] Alex: It's a simple SOW; I'll loop in legal after we confirm pilot scope.

[36:00] Samira: One more technical pointer—the AWD (adaptive weight) quant sometimes needs different dequant thresholds in runtime; Redwood runtime exposes per-model quant config for that. We'll include recommended config.

[37:00] Ethan: Let's plan a follow-up call to go through initial pilot results and kernel notes.
[37:05] Alex: We'll schedule for two weeks after pilot start—Samira will propose times.

[38:00] (crosstalk)
[38:12] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[38:16] Alex: Thanks all. We'll follow up with materials and the invite.

[38:30] End transcript (note: timestamps approximate; transcription contains minor mis-recognitions).
